tldr: We developed CQDC-Warp, a differentiable simulator that runs thousands of environments in parallel on GPUs. Coupled with MPC that only loosely specifies intended contact links, it achieves tens of times faster trajectory generation and higher success rates across multi-fingered in-hand rotation and whole-body tasks.
hero_caption: An overview of CQDC-Warp. Highly parallel on GPUs and fully differentiable, it quickly solves contact tasks across diverse robots—from multi-fingered in-hand manipulation to whole-body coordination in quadrupeds and humanoids.
overview:
Contact-rich manipulation, where robots repeatedly make and break complex contacts using their fingers or bodies, is essential for dexterous intelligence. However, contact transitions are discontinuous and highly non-convex. This makes automatically planning trajectories with techniques like Model Predictive Control (MPC) exceptionally difficult. Reinforcement learning requires vast amounts of trial and error, while traditional gradient-based methods have mostly relied on CPUs, suffering from slow compute times.

To solve this, the authors turned to the Convex Quasi-Dynamic Contact (CQDC) model, which omits transient oscillations to permit large simulation time steps. They incorporated compliant contact to handle deformation and introduced accurate inertial coupling. Then, they rebuilt it on NVIDIA Warp, a GPU-parallel framework, creating the differentiable simulator CQDC-Warp. On top of this, they introduced an approach where planners loosely guide motions with cost functions specifying which links should touch, leaving exact contact locations and friction forces to the physical simulation.

In evaluations across 17,408 trials on a 17-object Allegro Hand in-hand rotation benchmark, CQDC-Warp achieved a 79.8% success rate, significantly outperforming prior methods like CFree and IMPACT. It also sped up trajectory generation by 27x to 50x. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated its versatility with LEAP and Shadow hands, leveraging environmental contacts with tables and walls, bimanual manipulation, humanoid whole-body control, and real-world trajectory replay on a Sharpa hand.
contributions: Built CQDC-Warp, a GPU-parallel differentiable simulator extending quasi-dynamic contact models by incorporating compliant contact and joint-base inertial coupling.
Proposed contact-guided MPC, which avoids prescribing rigid contact-mode schedules and instead loosely specifies intended contact links, leaving geometry and friction to the dynamics.
Vastly outperformed existing methods in both success rate and planning speed on a 17-object in-hand rotation benchmark, and demonstrated successful trajectory replay on a real robot hand.

sections.heading: Why is planning dexterous contact so hard, and how can we solve it?
sections.summary: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is central to robot learning, but collecting data and planning motions remain notoriously difficult. This work breaks through by building a GPU simulator with thousands of parallel differentiable rollouts and using contact-guided MPC.
sections.details:
Dexterous object manipulation with multi-fingered hands is one of the most critical capabilities for general-purpose robotics. Modern robot learning demands large, diverse action datasets. However, human teleoperation is expensive and hindered by structural differences between human and robot hands, making data collection tough. Automatically synthesizing physically valid trajectories quickly and at scale would be a massive asset—both for direct execution and for downstream training data.

While reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved impressive milestones, it treats dynamics as a black box. This demands extensive trial and error and often leaves policies brittle to environmental shifts. In contrast, gradient-based planning leverages dynamic gradients to optimize action sequences efficiently. Yet, simultaneously optimizing continuous motion and discrete contact transitions causes the problem's non-convexity to explode.

As a practical middle ground, the authors adopted a contact-guided strategy: specify intended contacts—which robot links should touch the object—in advance, but leave the exact contact points, sticking, and sliding responses to the simulator. Previous differentiable simulators were either slow on CPUs or constrained to specific robot models on GPUs. In response, this work develops CQDC-Warp, making convex quasi-dynamic contact fully differentiable across thousands of parallel environments on a GPU to enable fast, accurate planning across diverse robot morphologies.

sections.heading: Lineage of rigid contact, differentiable simulators, and trajectory optimization
sections.summary: The authors review three key areas: rigid body contact models, differentiable simulation techniques, and contact-rich trajectory optimization. This work positions itself using cone complementarity problems, implicit differentiation with surrogate geometric gradients, and contact-guided single-shooting MPC.
sections.details:
### II-A Rigid Body Contact Models
Rigid contact models generally fall into two camps: classic penalty methods that push interpenetrations back with spring-dampers, and complementarity-based methods that strictly forbid penetration. Penalty methods often suffer from numerical instability when stiffness is high. Complementarity methods traditionally relied on Nonlinear Complementarity Problems (NCP) or Linear Complementarity Problems (LCP) with polyhedral friction cones. Recently, Cone Complementarity Problems (CCP) have gained traction because they preserve friction cones while relaxing normal constraints, allowing contact to be solved as convex optimization—forming the bedrock of CQDC.

### II-B Differentiable Contact Simulation
To compute dynamics gradients, one can either trace the entire computational graph using Automatic Differentiation (AD) or apply the Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) at the solution's convergence point. Unrolling iterative solvers with AD causes compute costs to scale with iteration count. In contrast, implicit differentiation directly solves a sensitivity system without backpropagating through solver steps, making it vastly more efficient. Another crucial piece is geometric gradients, which describe how contact points and normals shift with body poses. Because mesh collision detection produces non-differentiable boundaries across triangles, surrogate gradients—built from surface sample points to create smooth local gradients—have shown great promise. CQDC-Warp adopts both implicit differentiation and surrogate geometric gradients.

### II-C Contact-Rich Trajectory Optimization
Trajectory optimization approaches include single shooting, multiple shooting, and direct collocation. When handling contact, methods range from strictly pre-fixing contact mode schedules (like Crocoddyl) to fully discovering them automatically (contact-implicit). This work adopts a contact-guided single-shooting MPC backed by GPU rollouts. It strikes a practical balance: neither overly constraining contact modes nor leaving the solver entirely unguided.

sections.heading: Foundational theory: Quasi-dynamic models and differentiable collision detection
sections.summary: This section covers the Convex Quasi-Dynamic Contact (CQDC) baseline and surrogate geometric gradients. The keys lie in neglecting high-frequency transient vibrations to enable large time steps and smoothly approximating discrete collision queries.
sections.details:
### III-A CQDC: Convex Quasi-Dynamic Contact Model
CQDC is a convex, differentiable quasi-dynamic contact model introduced by Pang et al. In manipulation regimes dominated by friction and damping at low velocities, high-frequency oscillations from inertia (transient dynamics) can be neglected. Instead, motion can be modeled as transitions across quasi-static equilibria. This allows setting a much larger time step $h$ than standard dynamic simulators, enabling long-horizon planning with fewer steps. Control inputs are formulated as impedance target positions $u$. Contact forces and the resulting generalized displacement $\delta q$ are uniquely solved via a convex Second-Order Cone Program (SOCP).

### III-B Differentiable Collision Detection
Mesh collision detection algorithms like GJK and EPA find the closest witness points between geometries. However, which vertex or face is selected shifts discretely, cutting off gradient flow. Prior works such as DiffCollision resolved this by using standard collision detection in the forward pass while applying a soft-argmax (a weighted average scaled by a temperature parameter $\tau$) over surface point clouds during the backward pass. This constructs a smooth, differentiable surrogate function.

sections.heading: Designing CQDC-Warp: Bringing back compliant contact and inertial coupling
sections.summary: The authors extend CQDC by introducing compliant contact that allows deformation and refining the floating-base inertial coupling model. They also streamline contact geometry and solver derivatives, unlocking massive GPU parallelism via NVIDIA Warp.
sections.details:
### IV-A Incorporating Compliant Contact
Standard CQDC assumes completely rigid contact, causing the solver's numerical conditioning to degrade sharply during contact transitions. Here, the authors introduce a compliant contact model that permits deformation while preserving friction cone constraints. They introduce a compliance matrix $\mathbf{R} = \rho \mathbf{I}$ with $\rho > 0$ to tune contact stiffness. This formulation shares the convex structure of MuJoCo's compliant contact. By eliminating variables via cone projection, the formulation reduces to an unconstrained, strictly convex optimization problem. Solving this with a batched Newton method on GPUs drastically cuts iteration counts, boosting speed and stability.

### IV-B Refined Inertia Model
For floating-base platforms like quadrupeds or humanoids, inertial coupling between the base and joints—where moving joints exerts reaction forces on the base—is critical. Standard CQDC simplified inertia into block-diagonal terms, dropping this coupling and causing noticeable Sim-to-Sim discrepancies. CQDC-Warp retains the full generalized mass matrix $\mathbf{M}(q)$, accurately capturing the dynamic interplay between the base and articulated limbs.

### IV-C Surrogate Geometric Gradients for Contact
While DiffCollision smoothed witness points on two bodies separately with soft-argmax, recomputing contact normals and signed gaps required redundant gradient tracking. CQDC-Warp samples witness point pairs and uses a shared softmax weighting to estimate the contact midpoint $c$, contact normal $n$, and signed distance $g$ simultaneously in one cohesive surrogate gradient formulation.

### IV-D Implicit Differentiation and GPU Implementation
Gradients of the converged displacement $\delta q$ are computed using the Implicit Function Theorem on the KKT stationarity residuals. The core simulation is implemented using NVIDIA Warp, a Python-based framework for GPU kernels, built upon the batched architecture of MuJoCo-Warp. Both the forward Newton solver and the backward adjoint linear systems execute fully in parallel across thousands of environments on a single GPU.

captions.F2: Comparison of inertia models using a floating-base toy system. Standard CQDC (a) drops joint-base coupling, failing to move the base correctly. In contrast, the proposed refined model (b) closely reproduces the rigorous dynamic behavior of MuJoCo-Warp (c).

sections.heading: Contact-guided MPC: Generating intricate contacts from high-level intent
sections.summary: This section outlines the GPU-parallel MPC framework using CQDC-Warp as its internal model. Planners supply rough intents for which links should touch as soft costs, letting differentiable dynamics discover exact contact modes and forces.
sections.details:
### V-A Batched Receding Horizon Optimization
The MPC optimizes control input sequences (impedance target positions) across a finite horizon $H$ (default $H=5$ steps) by rolling out futures in CQDC-Warp. In each control cycle, the GPU runs 20 parallel gradient updates, executes only the first step of the best control sequence, and shifts forward to the next observation (Algorithm 1). For gradient updates, the authors apply block normalization across translation, rotation, and joint angle segments alongside a cosine-decayed learning rate. This prevents instability when balancing variables with different physical units.

### V-B Trajectory Cost Design
The MPC objective consists of three core components:
- **Pose Tracking Cost**: Guides the manipulated object toward a goal pose. To avoid vanishing gradients near the target, an error velocity penalty is added. Crucially, a stop-gradient is applied to the previous step's error, preventing the optimizer from artificially reducing velocity by warping past states.
- **Regularization Costs**: Penalizes excessive object velocities, joint limit violations, and the velocity and acceleration of control inputs to prevent abrupt or unnatural motions.
- **Contact Cost**: The centerpiece of the contact-guided approach. A distance cost encourages the signed distance $g$ between user-specified robot links and the object to match a target $g^*$ (typically zero). Anchor position costs can also be added to loosely tether contacts in world coordinates. Because these are soft costs, the sticking/sliding modes and precise contact points emerge naturally from simulated physics.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Dramatic speedups and broad robotic applications
sections.summary: CQDC-Warp crushed prior methods in success rate and speed on 17-object in-hand rotation. It demonstrated strong generality across three multi-fingered hands, environmental contacts, bimanual manipulation, whole-body control, and real-world execution.
sections.details:
### VI-A In-Hand Rotation Benchmark
Experiments ran on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. On an Allegro Hand benchmark rotating 17 distinct objects (1,024 trials per object, totaling 17,408 trials), CQDC-Warp reached an average success rate of 79.8%. It comfortably surpassed CPU-based sequential baselines: CFree achieved 73.7% and IMPACT reached 65.2%. Furthermore, its average trajectory generation time was just 0.794 seconds—delivering a 27.0x speedup over CFree (21.4 s) and a 50.2x speedup over IMPACT (39.8 s).
CQDC-Warp also translated smoothly to other morphologies: it achieved 79.88% on the 16-DoF LEAP Hand, 65.75% on the 22-DoF Shadow Hand, and a 54% success rate on a challenging box-flipping task.

### VI-B Diverse Robots and Contact Tasks
The framework extends far beyond single-hand manipulation:
- **Environmental Contacts**: Using a Shadow Hand, it pushed a bottle over against a table and lifted an object wedged between a floor and wall, achieving over 90% success.
- **Bimanual Manipulation**: Coordinating two Shadow Hands, it stabilized a bottle with one hand while unscrewing its cap by 90 degrees with the other (1024/1024 success), and lifted a truncated cone from both sides (1007/1024 success).
- **Whole-Body Control**: It solved sparse-target coordination tasks for floating-base systems, including a tripod stance on an A1 quadruped, bottle lifting with an armed GO2 quadruped, and squatting or bottle lifting with a G1 humanoid.
- **Real-World Replay**: Open-loop replay of a planned bottle-tilting trajectory on a real Sharpa Hand succeeded cleanly without dropping the object, confirming physical feasibility.

### VI-C Compute Throughput and Ablations
With 2,048 parallel environments, simulation throughput reached $2.06\times 10^5$ world-steps per second forward and $2.25\times 10^5$ backward—matching MuJoCo-Warp's forward speed ($2.24\times 10^5$). Looking purely at the contact solver, CQDC-Warp was 1,270x faster than GPU MOREAU and 10,800x faster than CPU Clarabel.
Ablation studies showed that removing geometric gradients caused a 2.44 percentage point drop in success. A horizon of $H=5$ proved optimal ($H=1$ yielded 0% success because it cannot anticipate future object motions).

captions.F3: Examples of diverse contact behaviors generated by CQDC-Warp: (a)–(d) show multi-fingered in-hand rotation, (e) and (f) depict manipulation leveraging tables and walls, (g) and (h) show bimanual coordination, and (i)–(l) demonstrate whole-body quadruped and humanoid control.
captions.F4: Real-world trajectory replay on a Sharpa hand. A contact trajectory for tilting a bottle synthesized by CQDC-Warp is stably and accurately reproduced in reality.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future work: Toward large-scale data generation for dexterous skills
sections.summary: CQDC-Warp proves to be a powerful tool for fast, accurate contact-rich manipulation. However, limitations remain around initial poses, cost weight tuning, and using the generated data for downstream learning.
sections.details:
This paper presented CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic simulator, alongside contact-guided MPC driven by soft contact intent costs. The framework demonstrates that trajectory optimization for contact-rich manipulation can achieve both dramatic computational speedups and wide task generality.

Nonetheless, notable limitations remain. First, because this is a local trajectory optimization approach, it still relies on reasonable initial poses and pre-specified contact intents (which links should touch). Its ability to handle long-horizon tasks with frequent contact re-grasping remains to be fully explored. Second, while parameters generalize well within a task family, switching robot platforms or tasks still requires manual tuning of cost weights. Finally, validating whether large sets of synthesized trajectories can effectively bootstrap downstream policy learning—via imitation learning or RL pre-training—remains an exciting direction for future research.

takeaways: Contact guidance—providing loose intent for which links should touch rather than fixing full contact schedules or searching unconstrained—is exceptionally practical.
Integrating compliant contact into a quasi-dynamic framework stabilizes numerical conditioning, enabling ultra-fast solutions via GPU-batched Newton methods.
For floating-base robots, preserving full joint-base inertial coupling in the generalized mass matrix is indispensable for dynamic simulation fidelity.
limitations: Relies on reasonable initial trajectories and pre-designed contact link intents, limiting its ability to discover contact transitions from scratch across long-horizon tasks.
Hyperparameters and objective cost weights still require manual tuning whenever robot morphologies, degrees of freedom, or task specifications change.
The downstream benefits of using generated trajectory datasets for large-scale robot policy training (such as imitation learning or RL pre-training) have not yet been evaluated.
